# Introduction

Can political bulletins tell us something about party's level of centralization?

# Theory

## Model

The setup goes as follows. A national party $P$ seeks to gain as many
votes as possible in order to win an election. To achieve this, it has
to convince the local population across the whole country to i) turn out
on the day of the election, and ii) vote for party $P$. To do this, the
party has resources that it can allocate across the different
constituencies to help promote certain candidates. The party $P$ also needs
to decide how *discretionary* its candidates can be in their campaign.
For simplicity, we will treat the allocation of resources as fixed for this
model, and focus exclusively on the *centralization* choice of party $P$.

The problem of centralization goes as follows. The leader ($L$) of
party $P$ does not know about the local needs and issues of all the
constituencies.  Therefore, by granting little discretionary power to
the candidates ($C$) running for its party, he runs the risk of alienating
part of the electorate. His priorities might be situated far from those
of the local population in constituency $d$.

On the other hand, the party leader can't delegate all the power and
discretionary choices to the candidates. Doing so would be
suboptimal, as his preferences might not be aligned with
those of all the candidates. Therefore, delegating all of his power to
the local candidates runs the risk of leaving these candidates to run on
"unwanted platforms". The party still wants to campaign on a relatively
similar platform. Therefore, the choice is to decide how far from the
party's national platform candidates can run.

The formalization goes as follows. In this game, we have one party leader
$L$ and $N$ candidates, one per constituency $d \in \{1, \dots, N\}$.
The party leader $L$ has utility preferences represented by
$u_L(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) = -\sum_{d=1}^{N} (x_d - \theta_d)^2$.
Here, $x_d$ represents the platform chosen by the candidate in
constituency $d$, and $\theta_d$ is the optimal point of constituency $d$.
Each constituency's optimal point is drawn i.i.d. from a distribution $F$,
$\theta_d \sim F$. The party leader doesn't observe the realization of
$\theta_d$, but he does know the distribution $F$.

The candidate in constituency $d$ has utility preferences represented by
$u_{C_d}(x_d, \theta_d, b) = -(x_d - \theta_d - b)^2$, where $x_d$ is
the candidate's platform, $\theta_d$ is the local optimal point, and $b$
is the bias, or disagreement, of the candidates with the party leader,
assumed common to all candidates.
Each candidate gets to observe $\theta_d$ before choosing their own 
platform $x_d$.

The game follows this timing: $L$ commits to a set of permitted
platforms $\mathcal{D}$; Nature draws $\theta_d$; candidate $d$ observes $\theta_d$; candidate $d$
chooses $x_d \in \mathcal{D}$.

## Literature

# Data

This project collects an original dataset using political bulletins in
Japan for the 2024, 2025, and 2026 lower house elections. The pipeline goes
as follow. We first developped a webscrapper to retrieve the election
bulletins from [go2senkyo.com](https://go2senkyo.com/). The website
compiles all the election bulletins across all districts retrieved from
each prefecture's electoral commission. The scrapper gets all the PDFs
files and store them locally. Once the files are downloaded, another 
script uses Claude API to segment all the PDFs into the candidates 
running inside district $d$. This approach is to facilitate the following
step, which is to use PDF parsing and OCR, and to increase the precision
of the information retrieved. About the parsing and the OCR, we used the
[Yomitoku](https://kotaro-kinoshita.github.io/yomitoku/en/) Python librairy
that is optimized for Japanese text and documents.

Once the parsing is done, we can store the information into a Pandas dataframe.
Each candidates (rows) have the following information attached to them: 
1) text from their election bulletin, 2) the number of paragraphs,
3) the number of headings, 4) the total number of characters (including both
Kanji and Kana).
